newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast regroups for 1998 cocoa fat debate.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast regroups for 1998 cocoa fat debate.

text.p: Cocoa producers will use a two-year respite to rally arguments and protect their interests against European Union (EU) plans to raise levels of non-cocoa fat usage, Ivory Coast's commodities minister said on Friday.
EU proposals to revise world Codex Alimentarius food standards to allow the move were deferred until 1998 this month, but will be debated in the EU parliament in January.
"This gives producers time to develop new arguments and form a new strategy," Guy-Alain Gauze told a news conference after returning from EU proposal hearings at Thun, Switzerland.
"The arguments (will be) impassionate and based on technical arguments," he added.
The world Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), asked by the EU to change chocolate standards in the Codex Alimentarius food standard list, put off a decision on October 3.
Gauze indicated the subject would be discussed soon by ministers reviewing the 1993 International Cocoa Agreement after a Cocoa Producers Alliance meeting next week in Gabon.
"We will talk about everything. What I haven't said here we can discuss there," Gauze told Reuters after the conference.
Gauze said processors and investors in Ivory Coast would be encouraged despite fears exported butter markets would be hit.
"The option of processing 50 percent of national production is irreversible," he said. Ivory Coast, the world's largest producer, now processes about 15-18 percent, of local beans.
Gauze said EU member states were not respecting their obligations under articles 32 and 33 of the 1993 International Cocoa Agreement (ICA).
The European parliament this week reviewed a Commission proposal to allow up to five percent vegetable fats in chocolate across the EU, subject to approval by individual governments.
Gauze said if current minimum levels of 18 percent cocoa butter and 25-30 percent of cocoa solids were not met products should be called other names than pure chocolate.

"Wine comes from vines. Chocolate exists because of cocoa beans," he said, and member states could proceed only if consumers were not mislead. "Labeling must be clear. How can consumers make a choice otherwise."

Gauze repeated figures given last month saying the EU plan would cause a 60,000-200,000 tonnes drop in EU cocoa bean demand, depending on the figures used, cutting producer receipts by 280 billion CFA francs. If the United States followed suit there would be additional losses of $90-113 million a year.
A Dutch study recently concluded that only 33,000 tonnes of cocoa beans, or 1.3 percent of world demand, would be substituted.
Gauze said even high quality substitute producers, which include nearby Mali and Burkina Faso, could suffer without clear packaging, naming, and contents detail rules.
"Substitutes can have the same molecular structure but completely different qualities," he said. "There is no way of detecting how much is being used so it is open to abuse," he added.
A French industry body this week urged the EU to push through the proposals which France still opposes.
